title: Challenge: build your own image from a Dockerfile
intro: A Dockerfile is already in this directory. Build it into an image, run it to test, then tag and push it to a registry, the everyday build-and-ship loop. (Commands are checked, not executed.)

steps.instruction: Build the Dockerfile in the current directory, tagging the image 'myapp:1.0'. Don't forget the build-context argument.
steps.success:
[+] Building 2.3s (8/8) FINISHED
 => [1/3] FROM docker.io/library/alpine:3.20
 => [2/3] COPY app /app
 => [3/3] RUN chmod +x /app
 => exporting to image
 => => naming to docker.io/library/myapp:1.0
steps.fail: docker build -t <name>:<tag> <context>. The context is usually '.' (the current directory).

steps.success:
REPOSITORY   TAG    IMAGE ID       SIZE
myapp        1.0    9b2c1a4d5e6f   8.1MB

steps.instruction: Run a throwaway container from your new image to test it (--rm cleans it up on exit).
steps.success: Hello from myapp! Running inside your freshly built image.
steps.fail: docker run --rm <image>. The --rm flag removes the container when it exits.

steps.instruction: Tag the image for a registry: registry.example.com/team/myapp:1.0.
steps.success: (no output) the registry tag now points at the same local image

steps.instruction: Push it to the registry so others (and your cluster) can pull it.
steps.success:
The push refers to repository [registry.example.com/team/myapp]
1.0: digest: sha256:7f3a9c... size: 1365
Pushed

done: Solved! build -> run -> tag -> push is the image lifecycle. The build context (that trailing '.') is what Docker sends to the daemon; tagging with a registry host is what lets you push and share it.
